Instrumental variables with treatment clusters

Abstract

Many policy evaluations include multiple unordered treatments. A common approach is to aggregate these treatments into clusters and apply instrumental variable (IV) methods at the treatment cluster level: The clusters are treated as binary treatments and the IV assumptions are invoked at the cluster level. This paper shows that IV with treatment clusters identifies a weighted average of local average treatment effects (LATEs) under a set of assumptions at the unclustered treatment level. When data on unclustered treatment choice is available, we propose testable necessary conditions for the causal interpretation of IV with treatment clusters. We illustrate our methods with empirical applications to the causal effects of fields of study aggregated into STEM and non-STEM clusters or eight broad study directions.

JEL: C36, C38, I23
Keywords: Multiple unordered treatments, Instrumental variables, Treatment clusters, Fields of study

1 Introduction

Many policy evaluations involve multiple unordered treatments, such as location decisions by firms or families (Chetty et al., 2016) or student fields of study choices (Altonji et al., 2016). Researchers often aggregate these treatments into clusters. For instance, STEM and non-STEM programs (Ng and Riehl, 2024), Business and non-Business majors (Andrews et al., 2017), or broad study directions (Dahl et al., 2023), all consist of fields of study such as Physics or Finance. When treatment choice is endogenous, instrumental variable (IV) methods may be used to estimate a local average treatment effect (LATE) of a cluster of treatments. A STEM degree is then considered as a binary treatment choice, and the IV assumptions are invoked at the cluster level. However, individuals choose among treatments within the clusters, and therefore the instruments may induce changes in treatment take up across and within clusters. Hence, treatments have to be considered at the unclustered level as otherwise violations of the IV assumptions may stay undetected (Imbens and Rubin, 2015). This raises the question of what parameter IV estimation at the cluster level is targeting, and under what conditions this parameter has a causal interpretation.

This paper studies IV estimation with treatments aggregated into clusters in a setting where both treatment and instrument are multi-valued unordered variables defined over the same support. We show that IV with clustered treatments identifies a weighted average of LATEs under a set of assumptions imposed at the unclustered treatment level. This weighted average includes the LATEs of all pairs of treatments across two clusters, and all instrument values associated with these clusters. The assumptions clarify which potential treatment choices have to be excluded, which does not directly follow from the IV assumptions of Imbens and Angrist (1994) invoked at the cluster level. The assumptions are less strict than the IV assumptions required for identifying LATEs between the unclustered treatments (Bhuller and Sigstad, 2024). We show that this result applies to settings with an arbitrary number of treatment clusters and a corresponding number of instruments. We also derive necessary conditions for a causal interpretation of the IV estimand with treatment clusters that are testable using data at the unclustered treatment level.

Treatment evaluation often considers clusters of treatments instead of the actual treatments for three reasons. First, administrative data on treatments with small enrollment numbers may not be disclosed due to privacy concerns. Second, the estimation of a large number of pairwise treatment effects may suffer from a lack of accuracy. Third, a large number of estimates may be less relevant if the policy is designed at a less fine-grained level. Our results are applicable to these settings, and help practitioners interpret the parameter targeted by an IV analysis at the cluster level, and justify the IV assumptions required for a causal interpretation of this parameter.

To illustrate the empirical relevance of our methods, we study the causal effect of clusters of fields of study on the number of study credit points. We have access to an administrative data set that includes four cohorts in the Portuguese public higher education system, from which we exploit a natural experiment to construct instruments in a fuzzy regression discontinuity design (RDD). We estimate treatment cluster effects using the STEM versus non-STEM classification and eight broad academic clusters defined according to the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED).

To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to analyze the causal interpretation of the IV estimand with clusters of multiple unordered treatments. In a related setting, but with an ordered multivalued treatment, Angrist and Imbens (1995); Marshall (2016); Andresen and Huber (2021) discuss the implications of binarising the multivalued treatment. Treatment clusters have also been discussed in combination with conditional independence assumptions. For instance, Lechner (2002) discusses how to estimate the effect of treatment clusters in this setting. Heiler and Knaus (2023) decompose treatment effect heterogeneity with two treatment clusters into heterogeneous treatment responses and heterogeneity in the actual treatment take up.

There is an extensive literature that aims to identify pairwise unclustered treatment effects in the presence of multiple unordered treatments. When using multiple instrumental variables, Behaghel et al. (2013); Kirkebøen et al. (2016); Dahl et al. (2023); Bhuller and Sigstad (2024); Heinesen et al. (2026) allow each instrument to induce the choice of only one particular treatment, which is more restrictive than the assumptions required for an analysis at the treatment cluster level. Heckman and Pinto (2018) and Pinto (2021) discuss alternative assumptions for identifying multiple (local) average treatment effects with multiple discrete instruments. Lee and Salanié (2018) and Mountjoy (2022) discuss this setting with continuous instruments. Blackwell (2017) discusses the identification of interaction effects between multiple treatments with binary instruments. Kline and Walters (2016) consider the multiple treatment case with one instrument.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 introduces the setting with IVs for multiple unordered treatments. Section 3 analyses IV estimation with treatment clusters. Section 4 derives testable necessary conditions for the identifying assumptions, and Section 5 extends the results to a fuzzy RDD. Section 6 illustrates the empirical relevance of our methods with fields of study as multiple unordered treatments. Section 7 concludes.

2 IV with multiple unordered treatments

Suppose we have a multi-valued unordered treatment D∈{1,…,J}D\in\{1,\dots,J\} and a multi-valued unordered instrument Z∈{1,…,J}Z\in\{1,\dots,J\}. Define the mutually exclusive binary treatments Dj=𝟙[D=j]D_{j}=\mathbbm{1}[D=j] and the mutually exclusive binary instruments Zj=𝟙[Z=j]Z_{j}=\mathbbm{1}[Z=j]. Note that D=∑j=1Jj×DjD=\sum_{j=1}^{J}j\times D_{j} and Z=∑j=1Jj×ZjZ=\sum_{j=1}^{J}j\times Z_{j}. This setting, in which treatment and instrument have the same number of values and use the same labels, is common in IV applications with multiple treatments (Bhuller and Sigstad, 2024). Section 3.1 discusses how distinct treatment and instrument supports can be accommodated in our treatment cluster framework. Treatments that are not mutually exclusive can always be made into mutually exclusive treatments by defining new categories for each combination of treatments.

Define YY as the observed outcome of interest. Suppose that the effect on YY of taking treatment jj compared to treatment kk is heterogeneous across individuals. The instrument Zj=1Z_{j}=1 if the policymaker intends to encourage take up of treatment jj, but in practice this initial encouragement may also induce individuals to take up other treatments l≠jl\neq j. We define D⁡(z)D(z) as the potential treatment choice when ZZ is externally set to zz, with z=1,…,Jz=1,\dots,J. The dummy variable Dj​(z)D_{j}(z) equals one if treatment jj is chosen if Z=zZ=z, and hence Dj=∑l=1JDj​(l)×ZlD_{j}=\sum_{l=1}^{J}D_{j}(l)\times Z_{l} for each jj. Similarly, we define Y⁡(d,z)Y(d,z) as the potential outcome when D=dD=d and Z=zZ=z, with d=1,…,Jd=1,\dots,J and z=1,…,Jz=1,\dots,J. We make the following standard IV assumptions:

Assumption 1 (IV assumptions).
  1. a.

    (Independence) Y⁡(d,z),D⁡(z)⟂ZY(d,z),D(z)\perp Z for all d,zd,z.

  2. b.

    (Exclusion) Y⁡(d,z)=Y⁡(d)Y(d,z)=Y(d) for all d,zd,z.

Analyzing treatment choice at the unclustered treatment level is not always possible. For instance, consider fields of study as the multiple unordered treatments. Obtaining administrative data on study enrollment at the field of study level may be infeasible, in particular due to privacy constraints with the emergence of smaller degrees. With many small degrees it is challenging to obtain accurate estimates for the pairwise treatment effects between the degrees. Moreover, a large number of treatment effect estimates may be less relevant if the policy is designed at a less granular level, such as the promotion of gender equality in STEM enrollment (Kahn and Ginther, 2018). In such cases, practitioners often aggregate treatments into clusters and analyze the causal effects between these treatment clusters.

3 IV with clustered treatment data

This section analyses IV estimation with treatment clusters. First, it shows under which assumptions the IV estimand with two treatment clusters identifies a causal parameter, and discusses the interpretation of this parameter. Second, it shows that the results extend to the two-stage least squares (TSLS) estimand with an arbitrary number of clusters.

3.1 The IV estimand with two treatment clusters

Suppose we have two mutually exclusive clusters of treatments S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}. Define D~1=∑n∈S1Dn\tilde{D}_{1}=\sum_{n\in S_{1}}D_{n}, which equals one if a treatment in cluster S1S_{1} is chosen and zero otherwise. Similarly, define Z~1=∑n∈S1Zn\tilde{Z}_{1}=\sum_{n\in S_{1}}Z_{n}, which equals one if there is an initial encouragement to take up treatment from cluster S1S_{1} and zero otherwise. We refer to DnD_{n} and ZnZ_{n} as the treatment and instrument at the unclustered treatment level, and to D~1\tilde{D}_{1} and Z~1\tilde{Z}_{1} as these objects at the treatment cluster level. Consider the IV estimand

β=Δ​𝔼​[Y|Z~1]Δ​𝔼​[D~1|Z~1],\displaystyle\beta=\frac{\Delta\mathbb{E}[Y|\tilde{Z}_{1}]}{\Delta\mathbb{E}[\tilde{D}_{1}|\tilde{Z}_{1}]}, (1)

Assumption 2 (Relevance).

Δ​𝔼​[D~1|Z~1]>0\Delta\mathbb{E}[\tilde{D}_{1}|\tilde{Z}_{1}]>0.

This imposes relevance only at the treatment cluster level. Hence, the instrument may have no effect on the probability of taking treatments at the unclustered level, as long as it has a nonzero effect on the probability of taking treatment from cluster S1S_{1}.

We assume that the estimand in (1) is considered when the effect of taking treatment from cluster S1S_{1} compared to taking treatment from cluster S2S_{2} is of interest. A key identification challenge is that individuals may respond in various ways to the instrument. To describe this heterogeneity in responses, we follow Heckman and Pinto (2018) and define a response type as a vector of potential treatment choices for ZZ fixed at each value of its support: (D⁡(1),D⁡(2),…,D⁡(J))(D(1),D(2),\dots,D(J)). We refer to all response types who take treatment ll if Z=jZ=j and treatment mm if Z=kZ=k as (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=l,D(k)=m). Similarly, (D⁡(j)∈S1,D⁡(k)∈S2)(D(j)\in S_{1},D(k)\in S_{2}) describes all types who take treatment from S1S_{1} if Z=jZ=j and treatment from S2S_{2} if Z=kZ=k.

It does not, however, rule out the response types in B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}. This excludes the response types (D⁡(j)∈S2,D⁡(k)∈S1)(D(j)\in S_{2},D(k)\in S_{1}), which are also excluded by cluster monotonicity, and in addition it excludes (D⁡(j)∈S1,D⁡(k)∈S1)(D(j)\in S_{1},D(k)\in S_{1}), both with D⁡(j)≠D⁡(k)D(j)\neq D(k), j∈S1j\in S_{1}, and k∈S2k\in S_{2}. The classical monotonicity assumption with a single binary treatment and instrument has similar implications: It excludes the response type (D⁡(j)=k,D⁡(k)=jD(j)=k,D(k)=j), which represents all individuals for whom Z=jZ=j makes it less likely to take up treatment jj.

The plausibility of Assumption 3 depends on how treatments are grouped into clusters and how individuals respond to particular encouragements. Suppose that S1={1,2}S_{1}=\{1,2\} is a STEM cluster with Physical sciences (1) and Engineering (2), and S2={3,4}S_{2}=\{3,4\} a non-STEM cluster. Assumption 3 allows a STEM offer to induce enrollment in any STEM field, provided that the non-STEM offer induces enrollment in a non-STEM field. For example, (D⁡(1)=2,D⁡(3)=4)(D(1)=2,D(3)=4) is allowed: a student may enroll in Engineering when offered Physical sciences if they enroll in a non-STEM field following a non-STEM offer.

The assumption instead rules out a STEM offer inducing enrollment in a different STEM field from the one chosen following a non-STEM offer. For example, it rules out (D⁡(1)=1,D⁡(3)=2)(D(1)=1,D(3)=2), where a student enrolls in Physical sciences when offered Physical sciences but in Engineering when offered a non-STEM field. If treatments within a cluster are similar and switching costs are lower within than across clusters, such response types may be less likely: a student who enrolls in Physical sciences following a Physical sciences offer may also do so when entering STEM is more costly, yielding (D⁡(1)=1,D⁡(3)=1)(D(1)=1,D(3)=1), while a student able to reach Engineering following a non-STEM offer may also do so following a Physical sciences offer, yielding (D⁡(1)=2,D⁡(3)=2)(D(1)=2,D(3)=2).

where a=1a=1 and b=2b=2.

Since ∑j∈S1∑k∈S2∑l∈S1∑m∈S2λj​k​l​m=1\sum_{j\in S_{1}}\sum_{k\in S_{2}}\sum_{l\in S_{1}}\sum_{m\in S_{2}}\lambda_{jklm}=1 and 0≤λj​k​l​m≤10\leq\lambda_{jklm}\leq 1, β{\beta} is a weighted average of LATEs Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm}. The weighted average is taken over all possible pairs of treatments with one treatment from S1S_{1} and one from S2S_{2}, and for each of those treatment pairs all possible pairs of instruments between S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}.

The LATE Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm} equals the causal effect of treatment l∈S1l\in S_{1} compared to treatment m∈S2m\in S_{2}, for the response types (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=l,D(k)=m). Although Theorem 1 shows that under Assumptions 1 to 4 the weighted average of the LATEs is identified, the LATEs Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm} are not necessarily identified under these assumptions. The weights λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm} show which LATEs Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm} contribute the most to β{\beta}. The weight λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm} represents the normalized proportion of response types (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=l,D(k)=m) with j,l∈S1j,l\in S_{1} and k,m∈S2k,m\in S_{2}. The weight is normalized by the cumulative proportion of all these response types.

Theorem 1 delivers a transparent expression for the IV estimand in terms of LATEs using that treatment and instrument have the same number of values and the same labels. This restriction can be weakened if instrument values can be partitioned into sets TcT_{c} associated with treatment clusters ScS_{c}, without requiring |Tc|=|Sc||T_{c}|=|S_{c}| or the same labels. The results then extend by replacing instrument indices j∈Scj\in S_{c} by z∈Tcz\in T_{c}. If there are multiple instruments at the treatment cluster level with two clusters, the IV specification is overidentified. This changes the weighting structure in Theorem 1, and a causal interpretation generally requires additional restrictions of the type studied by Bhuller and Sigstad (2024).

3.2 The TSLS estimand with multiple treatment clusters

Suppose we have c=1,…,Cc=1,\dots,C mutually exclusive clusters of treatments ScS_{c}. Define the set S={Sc}c=1CS=\{S_{c}\}_{c=1}^{C} that includes all clusters. Define the CC-dimensional vectors 𝐙~𝐛=(1,Z~1,…​Z~b−1,Z~b+1,…,Z~C)′\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b}}=(1,\tilde{Z}_{1},\dots\tilde{Z}_{b-1},\tilde{Z}_{b+1},\dots,\tilde{Z}_{C})^{\prime} and 𝐃~𝐛=(1,D~1,…,D~b−1,D~b+1,…,D~C)′\mathbf{\tilde{D}_{b}}=(1,\tilde{D}_{1},\dots,\tilde{D}_{b-1},\tilde{D}_{b+1},\dots,\tilde{D}_{C})^{\prime}, where Z~c=∑n∈ScZn\tilde{Z}_{c}=\sum_{n\in S_{c}}Z_{n} and D~c=∑n∈ScDn\tilde{D}_{c}=\sum_{n\in S_{c}}D_{n}. Consider the TSLS estimand

β𝐛=𝔼​[𝐙~𝐛​𝐃~𝐛′]−1​𝔼​[𝐙~𝐛​Y],\displaystyle\mathbf{\beta_{b}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b}}\mathbf{\tilde{D}_{b}}^{\prime}]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b}}Y], (7)

where β𝐛=(β0​b,β1​b,…,βb−1,b,βb+1,b​…,βC​b)\mathbf{\beta_{b}}=(\beta_{0b},\beta_{1b},\dots,\beta_{b-1,b},\beta_{b+1,b}\dots,\beta_{Cb}). Note that β12\beta_{12} equals β\beta in (1) if C=2C=2. With more than two treatment clusters, the relevance condition in Assumption 2 has to be generalized to the condition that 𝔼⁡[𝐃~𝐛​𝐙~𝐛′]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{\tilde{D}_{b}}\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b}}^{\prime}] has full rank.

We assume (7) is considered if the effect of taking treatment from cluster ScS_{c} compared to taking treatment from cluster SbS_{b} is of interest, for c=1,…,Cc=1,\dots,C. For instance, the clusters can represent fields of study aggregated to broader study areas. Note that β𝐛\mathbf{\beta_{b}} can be considered for any b=1,…,Cb=1,\dots,C, and hence comparing to treatment cluster SbS_{b} is without loss of generality.

Table 2 describes all response types with D⁡(j)≠D⁡(k)D(j)\neq D(k) and more than two treatment clusters. The first four types are similar to the ones in Table 1 with a=1a=1 and b=2b=2: These individuals only take treatment from SaS_{a} and/or SbS_{b} if the instrument is fixed at values from the clusters SaS_{a} and SbS_{b}. With more than two treatment clusters, we can define five additional response types to instrument values j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. First, (D⁡(j)∉{Sa,Sb},D⁡(k)∈Sa)(D(j)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\},D(k)\in S_{a}) are individuals for whom Z∈SaZ\in S_{a} makes it less likely to take treatment from SaS_{a}, and are thus ruled out by Assumption 3. Second, the types (D⁡(j)∈Sb,D⁡(k)∉{Sa,Sb})(D(j)\in S_{b},D(k)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}), (D⁡(j)∉{Sa,Sb},D⁡(k)∈Sb)(D(j)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\},D(k)\in S_{b}), and (D⁡(j)∉{Sa,Sb},D⁡(k)∉{Sa,Sb})(D(j)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\},D(k)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}) represent individuals for whom D⁡(j)≠D⁡(k)D(j)\neq D(k) and both D⁡(j)D(j) and D⁡(k)D(k) are outside SaS_{a}. These are ruled out by Assumption 4. Third, (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)∉{Sa,Sb})(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}) are types who are not prevented by Assumptions 3 and 4, and therefore pose an additional identification problem in the multiple treatment cluster setting.

To prevent these response types, we introduce the following additional assumption.

Assumption 5 (Control group).

If there is an l∈Sal\in S_{a} for which Dl​(j)=1D_{l}(j)=1, then Dn​(k)=0D_{n}(k)=0 for all j∈Saj\in S_{a}, k∈Sbk\in S_{b}, and n∉{Sa,Sb}n\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}.

This assumption states that obtaining a treatment in SaS_{a} when the instrument is in SaS_{a} implies that no treatment outside SaS_{a} or SbS_{b} can be obtained when the instrument is in SbS_{b}. It follows that the types (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)∉{Sa,Sb})(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b} are excluded.

Assumption 5 may hold in settings with one or more control groups among the JJ treatments. Without loss of generality, we assume these control groups to be in SbS_{b}. Individuals may obtain the control when not encouraged to enroll in any other treatment than the control. For instance, Duflo et al. (2007) discuss randomized control trials with multiple treatment arms in development economics, where the control group typically receives no intervention. Behaghel et al. (2013) analyze a job market activation program with multiple treatment arms where the control group receives standard services. In the absence of a control group, the literature follows Kirkebøen et al. (2016) and Dahl et al. (2023): They assume that individuals have a preference ranking over treatments, which is revealed before ZZ is determined. Let rmr_{m} denote the treatment that received rank mm. Then Assumption 5 may hold in the subsample of individuals whose next-best treatment, r2r_{2}, belongs to SbS_{b}. Note that Assumption 5 allows for D⁡(j)=D⁡(k)D(j)=D(k) and does not require D⁡(k)=kD(k)=k for any response types, which makes it less restrictive than the next-best assumption formulated at the unclustered treatment level by Kirkebøen et al. (2016). Bhuller and Sigstad (2024) also discuss that the latter assumption can be relaxed to allow for D⁡(j)=D⁡(k)D(j)=D(k).

Under Assumptions 3 to 5, the only response types with D⁡(j)≠D⁡(k)D(j)\neq D(k) are those satisfying (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)∈Sb)(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)\in S_{b}) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. As in the two cluster case, this allows the instrument Z=jZ=j (Z=kZ=k) with initial encouragement for treatment jj (kk) to also induce take up of other treatments within the same cluster. Hence, βa​b\beta_{ab} in (7) has a similar causal interpretation as β\beta in (1), and boils down to the same expression with C=2C=2:

Theorem 2 (Causal interpretation TSLS estimand).


Under Assumptions 1-5, it holds for β𝐛=(β0​b,β1​b,…,βb−1,b,βb+1,b,…,βC​b)′\mathbf{\beta_{b}}=(\beta_{0b},\beta_{1b},\dots,\beta_{b-1,b},\beta_{b+1,b},\dots,\beta_{Cb})^{\prime} in (7) that

βa​b=∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sb∑l∈Sa∑m∈Sbλj​k​l​m​Δj​k​l​m,\displaystyle\beta_{ab}=\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{l\in S_{a}}\sum_{m\in S_{b}}\lambda_{jklm}\Delta_{jklm}, (8)

with a=1,…,b−1,b+1,…,Ca=1,\dots,b-1,b+1,\dots,C, and λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm} and Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm} defined in (4)-(6).

The proof is deferred to Section A.2. From hereon, we present results for an arbitrary number of clusters CC, and note that the results hold for C=2C=2 without Assumption 5.

Theorems 1 and 2 have direct implications for IV estimation with treatment clusters. Applying IV at the cluster level without specifying assumptions at the unclustered treatment level leaves violations unnoticed (Imbens and Rubin, 2015), and complicates the discussion of the validity of these assumptions. Our results allow researchers to precisely consider the validity of the required assumptions. Furthermore, they show that the parameter targeted by IV estimation at the cluster level has a well-defined causal interpretation as a weighted average of LATEs under appropriate assumptions, clarifying which LATEs contribute and the weight they receive. In Appendix B, we provide three strategies for obtaining further insights into the components of this weighted average.

4 Testable conditions

The estimand in (7) only requires data at the treatment cluster level. If data at the unclustered treatment level is available, necessary conditions of the identifying assumptions can be tested. It follows from Theorem 2 that in the absence of certain response types, the estimand in (7) has a causal interpretation. Table 2 summarizes which types are excluded by the underlying assumptions: Only types described by D⁡(j)∈SaD(j)\in S_{a} with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and D⁡(k)∈SbD(k)\in S_{b} with k∈Sbk\in S_{b} are allowed. This results in the following necessary conditions.

Proposition 1 (Necessary conditions causal interpretation).


Let AA be any subset of the support of YY, under Assumption 1 it holds that

ϕl​j​kA\displaystyle\phi_{ljk}^{A} =𝔼⁡[𝕀Y∈A​Dl|Z=j]−𝔼⁡[𝕀Y∈A​Dl|Z=k]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}|Z=j]-\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}|Z=k] (9)
=ℙ⁡[Y⁡(l)∈A,D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)≠l]−ℙ⁡[Y⁡(l)∈A,D⁡(j)≠l,D⁡(k)=l],\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[Y(l)\in A,D(j)=l,D(k)\neq l]-\mathbb{P}[Y(l)\in A,D(j)\neq l,D(k)=l],

with the necessary conditions for the causal interpretation of βa​b\beta_{ab} in Theorem 2:

  1. 1.

    ϕl​j​kA≥0\phi_{ljk}^{A}\geq 0 if l,j∈Sal,j\in S_{a}, k∈Sbk\in S_{b}, and Assumption 3 holds.

  2. 2.

    ϕl​j​kA≤0\phi_{ljk}^{A}\leq 0 if l,k∈Sbl,k\in S_{b}, j∈Saj\in S_{a}, and Assumptions 3 and 4 hold.

  3. 3.

    ϕl​j​kA=0\phi_{ljk}^{A}=0 if l∉{Sa,Sb}l\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}, j∈Saj\in S_{a}, k∈Sbk\in S_{b}, and Assumptions 3-5 hold.

Suppose that S1={1,2}S_{1}=\{1,2\}, S2={3,4}S_{2}=\{3,4\}, j=1j=1, and k=3k=3, and that Assumption 1 holds. Proposition 1 requires ϕ1,1,3A≥0\phi^{A}_{1,1,3}\geq 0 and ϕ2,1,3A≥0\phi^{A}_{2,1,3}\geq 0 under Assumption 3, while the corresponding quantities for treatments 3 and 4 must be nonpositive under Assumptions 3 and 4. Hence, the unclustered data may reveal violations that would be invisible from the cluster level data alone.

Depending on the support of YY, the conditions in Proposition 1 may pose an infinite number of (in)equalities. Mourifié and Wan (2017) show that such conditions can be written as conditional moment inequalities with YY as the conditioning variable instead of ZZ, allowing them to be tested using the intersection bounds framework of Chernozhukov et al. (2013). Bai et al. (2025) follow the same strategy for testing IV assumptions with multiple unordered treatments without clusters.

The Stata package clrtest by Chernozhukov et al. (2015) enables joint testing of the conditional moment inequalities within each estimation sample. Mourifié and Wan (2017) discuss the implementation of the multiple testing procedure of Holm (1979) when the clrtest is used to test the conditions across a large number of samples. Statistical power may be further improved by testing the conditions across covariate-specific subsamples using machine learning (Farbmacher et al., 2022).

Failure to reject the necessary conditions in Proposition 1 is not sufficient to conclude that Assumptions 1 and 3 to 5 hold. For instance, under Assumption 1, it may be the case that ℙ⁡[Y⁡(l)∈A,D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)≠l]>ℙ⁡[Y⁡(l)∈A,D⁡(j)≠l,D⁡(k)=l]>0\mathbb{P}[Y(l)\in A,D(j)=l,D(k)\neq l]>\mathbb{P}[Y(l)\in A,D(j)\neq l,D(k)=l]>0, which violates Assumption 3 while ϕl​j​kA≥0\phi_{ljk}^{A}\geq 0. By contrast, a rejection of the necessary conditions implies that the assumptions required for the causal interpretation of βa​b\beta_{ab} are violated. However, the decomposition of the IV estimand in Lemma 1 implies that the resulting bias may be small. For instance, the response types that violate the assumptions may receive little weight in the IV estimand, or their corresponding LATEs are similar to those included in the causal estimand.

Researchers may use rejections of specific necessary conditions to find clusters that do meet the assumptions, for instance by sequentially testing the necessary conditions. However, this approach introduces a pre-testing problem when inferring the treatment effect estimates, and may yield classifications for which the assumptions cannot be rejected, rather than classifications for which the assumptions actually hold. Researchers may therefore prefer to use the falsification tests to check the validity of a classification motivated by the empirical context or economic theory.

5 Fuzzy RDD with treatment clusters

This section provides an expression for the TSLS estimand with treatment clusters in a fuzzy regression discontinuity design. Fuzzy RDDs are commonly used in settings with multiple unordered treatments and revealed preference rankings over treatments. This is also the setting in Section 6.

In a fuzzy RDD, the instrument ZZ is determined by the value of a continuous running variable lying on either side of a fixed cutoff. We analyze the setting where the running variable induces encouragement toward the multiple unordered treatments as follows:

Z={r1S≥0,r2S<0,\displaystyle Z=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}r_{1}&S\geq 0,\\ r_{2}&S<0,\end{array}\right.

where rmr_{m} is the treatment receiving rank mm, and SS is the running variable minus the cutoff, with a density that is continuous and strictly positive at S=0S=0.

The fuzzy RDD replaces Assumption 1(a) by the local continuity assumption (Dong, 2018; Hahn, Todd, and Van der Klaauw, 2001):

Assumption 6 (Continuity).

Y⁡(d,z)Y(d,z) and D⁡(z)D(z) are continuous in SS at S=0S=0 for all d,zd,z.

This assumption implies that individuals just below and above the cutoff have similar potential outcomes. We control for smooth variation in the running variable with a polynomial function of the running variable fh​(S)f_{h}(S) with fh​(0)=0f_{h}(0)=0 within a bandwidth hh. This ensures that the fuzzy RDD estimand is identified from the discontinuity at the cutoff, rather than also capturing smooth relationships between the running variable and DD or YY (Imbens and Lemieux, 2008).

We extend the TSLS estimand in (7) to the RDD. Define the pp-dimensional vector 𝐗h=(𝐅′,𝐁h′)\mathbf{X}_{h}=(\mathbf{F}^{\prime},\mathbf{B}_{h}^{\prime}), where 𝐅\mathbf{F} includes the fixed effects fj​kf_{jk} that equal one if (r1,r2)=(j,k)(r_{1},r_{2})=(j,k) and zero otherwise, with j≠k∈Sbj\neq k\in S_{b}, and 𝐁h′\mathbf{B}_{h}^{\prime} includes the basis functions of the polynomial function fh​(S)f_{h}(S). The TSLS estimand equals

(δ𝐛𝐡′,β𝐛𝐡′)′=𝔼h[𝐙~𝐛,𝐡𝐃~𝐛,𝐡]′−1𝔼h[𝐙~𝐛,𝐡Y],\displaystyle(\mathbf{\delta_{b}^{h}}^{\prime},\mathbf{\beta_{b}^{h}}^{\prime})^{\prime}=\mathbb{E}_{h}[\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b,h}}\mathbf{\tilde{D}_{b,h}}{}^{\prime}]^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{h}[\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b,h}}Y], (12)

where 𝐙~𝐛,𝐡=(𝐗h′,𝐙~𝐛)′\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b,h}}=(\mathbf{X}_{h}^{\prime},\mathbf{\tilde{Z}_{b}})^{\prime}, 𝐃~𝐛,𝐡=(𝐗h′,𝐃~𝐛)′\mathbf{\tilde{D}_{b,h}}=(\mathbf{X}_{h}^{\prime},\mathbf{\tilde{D}_{b}})^{\prime}, and 𝔼h[A]=𝔼[A∣|S|≤h,r2∈Sb]\mathbb{E}_{h}[A]=\mathbb{E}[A\mid|S|\leq h,r_{2}\in S_{b}]. If each cluster contains only one treatment, this boils down to the fuzzy RDD estimand with unclustered treatments, and hence the results in this section also hold without treatment clusters. The estimand in (12) corresponds to the TSLS estimand of the equations:

Y\displaystyle Y =∑k∈Sb∑l≠kνl​kh​fl​k+∑a≠bβa​bh​D~a+fh,b​(S)+εh,b,\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{l\neq k}\nu_{lk}^{h}f_{lk}+\sum_{a\neq b}\beta_{ab}^{h}\tilde{D}_{a}+f_{h,b}(S)+\varepsilon_{h,b}, (13)

6 Application with fields of study

This section illustrates the empirical relevance of our methods in a setting with fields of study as multiple unordered treatments. We consider a natural experiment in the Portuguese public higher education system to study the effect of fields of study on the achieved number of study credit points.

6.1 Context and empirical specification

In the final year of high school, prospective students in Portugal apply to public higher education via a centralized admission process. Only 17 percent of the students use a different enrollment system to enroll into private higher education (Pordata, 2022). Applicants apply to a field and institution simultaneously, which we will refer to as a course (e.g., Law at the University of Lisbon). Applicants submit a ranking of up to six courses based on their preferences. Each course has a quota of students it can admit and ranks its applicants by a score based on high school and national exam grades. Because courses weight these components differently, application scores are applicant-course specific. Using these rankings and quotas, a deferred acceptance mechanism similar to the college-proposing Gale-Shapley algorithm (Gale and Shapley, 1962) matches each applicant to at most one course (DGES, 2019). Appendix C.1 describes this mechanism in more detail.

6.1.1 Course cutoffs, instruments, and next-best fields of study

The admission mechanism generates ex-ante unknown application-score cutoffs for each course. Each cutoff represents the lowest score that qualifies an applicant to receive an offer from that course. We construct the preferred and next-best fields from the course cutoffs, application scores, and submitted rankings. First, we retain applicants who rank courses from at least two different fields. Second, we construct preference blocks by assigning the same rank to consecutive courses in the submitted ranking that belong to the same field. Third, we consider the applicant’s matched block and the blocks immediately above and below it. We retain the block below only if the applicant scores above the cutoff for at least one course in that block, ensuring that it represents a feasible alternative. We drop applicants with no available adjacent block. If both adjacent blocks are available, we retain the block above and the matched block.

For these applicants, the higher-ranked retained block defines the preferred field r1r_{1}, while the lower-ranked block defines the next-best field r2r_{2}. These fields are local alternatives around the relevant course cutoff and need not correspond to the first two courses or fields in the submitted ranking.

Let 𝒬1\mathcal{Q}_{1} denote the set of courses in the preferred block, and let sqs_{q} and cqc_{q} denote the applicant’s score and the cutoff for course qq, respectively. We define the running variable as S=maxq∈𝒬1⁡{sq−cq}S=\max_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{1}}\{s_{q}-c_{q}\}. Thus, S≥0S\geq 0 indicates that the applicant clears the cutoff for at least one course in the preferred block, whereas S<0S<0 indicates that none of these cutoffs is cleared. The applicant receives an offer from field jj, and the instrument ZjZ_{j} equals one, if jj is the preferred field and the applicant clears the cutoff for at least one course in that block. The cutoff therefore represents either a single course-specific cutoff or the boundary formed by multiple course-specific cutoffs within the preferred block, and the binary representation in (5) applies.

Table 3 illustrates the construction of the preferred and next-best fields and the running variable. Panel A shows an applicant who ranks two courses in field jj, followed by two courses in field kk. The courses in each field form a preference block. The applicant does not clear the cutoff for the first-ranked course in field jj but exceeds the cutoff for the second-ranked course by 0.1 points. Because the running variable is the maximum re-centered score among all courses in the preferred block, it equals S=0.1S=0.1. The applicant also clears the cutoff for the highest-ranked course in field kk, making the remaining scores in that block irrelevant. Field jj is therefore the preferred field, field kk is the next-best field, and the applicant receives an offer from field jj.

Panel B summarizes and compares this applicant to another applicant with the same preferred and next-best fields who falls 0.1 points below the relevant cutoff for field jj but clears a course cutoff in field kk. The two applicants therefore have S=0.1S=0.1 and S=−0.1S=-0.1 and receive offers from fields jj and kk, respectively. The fuzzy RDD compares applicants immediately above and below these re-centered cutoffs. Because courses combine a field and an institution, crossing a cutoff may change both. Our field effects therefore include effects associated with any accompanying change in institution.

Our preferred and next-best fields may differ from students’ true preferences for three reasons. First, they represent local alternatives around a particular cutoff and need not be the two highest-ranked fields in the submitted ranking. Second, applicants can rank at most six courses, which may induce them to include safe options near the end of their rankings. These first two concerns appear limited in our setting because, for 88% of the sample, r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} coincide with the first- and second-ranked fields in the submitted ranking. Third, the college-proposing Gale-Shapley mechanism is not strategy proof from the applicants’ perspective. Applicants may have incentives to misreport their preferences beyond the first-ranked course (Roth, 1982), potentially introducing error into r2r_{2}.

Bertanha et al. (2026) discuss how strategic misreporting of preferences complicates identification of causal parameters that depend on true preferences. They also show that strategic reporting may violate the RD continuity assumption. They develop a partial identification approach robust to such behavior in a sharp RDD but leave identification in a fuzzy RDD with “multiple compliance types” to future work. Although we cannot rule out strategic reporting, the balancing and bunching tests reported below do not indicate violations of the RD continuity assumption.

6.1.2 Data and classifications of fields of study

We have access to an administrative data set that includes four cohorts in the Portuguese public higher education system. From the application data we observe each applicant’s submitted course ranking, application scores, and matched course, on top of all course cutoffs. From the student outcome data we observe a student’s enrolled course, whether a student is active in the first, second, or third year of that course, and the achieved number of study credits in each year for that course. Appendix C.2 provides further details on the data and sample construction and presents some descriptive statistics.

Study credits are measured using the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS), which facilitates the accumulation and transfer of learning achievements across European universities. ECTS credits represent learning outcomes and the estimated workload required to achieve them. One ECTS credit typically represents 25 to 30 hours of intended workload, while 60 ECTS correspond to one academic year, or 1,500 to 1,800 hours of workload. Four and eight ECTS typically correspond to a medium-sized and large course, respectively. These standards apply across institutions and fields, making ECTS comparable in terms of intended workload, but not in terms of content, difficulty, or quality.

We interpret achieved ECTS as a measure of study progress rather than a measure of skills or welfare: achieving more credits represents the completion of more intended workload and greater progress toward degree completion, but does not necessarily imply more skill development, enjoyment, or future earnings. Universities in several European countries eventually dismiss students who obtain insufficient credits (Sneyers and Witte, 2018). In those settings, differences in academic progress could affect continued enrollment. However, dropout in Portugal is low, so this is not the focus of this application.

The Portuguese education authorities organize courses into 22 fields of study following the 2-digit International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) from UNESCO Institute for Statistics (2012). Column (1) of Table 4 shows the 22 fields of study, which we define as our unclustered treatments. Column (2) classifies the 22 fields into two clusters according to the STEM versus non-STEM distinction from OECD (2022). Column (3) constructs eight clusters using the ISCED 1-digit classification: fields that share the same first digit in their 2-digit classification are grouped together in a broader field.

6.1.3 Empirical specification

We estimate the fuzzy RD model as specified in (13)-(14) using the sample analogue of (12). For treatment cluster SbS_{b}, the estimation sample contains students whose next-best field belongs to SbS_{b}. For the unclustered field classification, where each cluster contains one field, Column (4) of Table 4 reports these estimation samples. For the STEM and ISCED classifications, we pool the samples over all next-best fields within the same cluster.

The outcome variable YY equals the number of study credits collected in the second year of a student’s course. The treatment variable D~a=∑j∈SaDj\tilde{D}_{a}=\sum_{j\in S_{a}}D_{j} equals one if the student’s second-year course enrollment corresponds to a field in cluster SaS_{a}. The instrument Z~c=∑l∈ScZl\tilde{Z}_{c}=\sum_{l\in S_{c}}Z_{l} equals one if the student prefers a field in cluster ScS_{c} and has an application score above one of its course cutoffs. Clustering therefore pools discontinuities around the re-centered course-specific cutoffs. The fixed effect fj​kf_{jk} equals one if the preferred and next-best field of the student are jj and kk, respectively.

The function fh​(S)f_{h}(S) is approximated by a first-degree polynomial, such that fh​(S)=γ​Sf_{h}(S)=\gamma S, and we do not apply a bandwidth to our sample. Section C.3 shows that our results are robust against the inclusion of higher order polynomials and the use of smaller bandwidths. Furthermore, we report on balancing and bunching tests leading to the conclusion that we cannot reject the RD continuity assumption. We use heteroskedasticity robust standard errors and apply the Holm (1979) correction to account for multiple hypothesis tests within each estimation sample.

Because the treatment variable is defined as second-year course enrollment, our estimation sample is restricted to students with observed second-year enrollment. The local continuity assumption then requires that the course offer does not affect selection into this sample near the cutoff. Non-enrollment and dropout are relatively low in Portugal. Approximately 10% of applicants do not enroll in public higher education in their first year (DGES, 2018), while approximately 2.5% of those who enroll drop out before the second year (Figueiredo et al., 2026). The latter is consistent with Portugal’s fixed admission quotas, which give little incentive to induce dropout after admission. These rates suggest limited attrition, while balancing and bunching tests reveal no significant irregularities around the cutoff. Together, these findings are reassuring, but do not entirely rule out offer-induced selection near the cutoff.

With our treatment definition, the exclusion restriction also requires that course offers affect second-year credits only through the second-year field of enrollment. Two potential violations merit discussion. First, offers may affect the institution without changing the field, in which case differences in institutional characteristics could directly affect credits. Such effects are likely to be limited as Portuguese public institutions offering the same fields have similar curricula and academic requirements. Second, offers may change first-year field without changing the second-year field. If these earlier experiences directly affect second-year credits, exclusion is violated. A formal analysis of these multiple treatment stages is beyond the scope of this paper, but Angrist et al. (2025) discuss identification in these settings with a single instrumental variable.

6.1.4 Identifying assumptions with treatment clusters

The set of identifying assumptions required for a causal interpretation of the TSLS estimand with treatment clusters depends on the number of clusters. In addition to the standard IV assumptions, the STEM classification with two treatment clusters requires Assumptions 3 and 4. We discuss the plausibility of these two assumptions in turn.

First, consider a student whose next-best field is in the non-STEM cluster, such as Personal services, and whose preferred field is in the STEM cluster, such as Physical sciences. A score above the cutoff implies an offer to enroll in Physical sciences rather than Personal services. Assumption 3 rules out students for whom a Physical sciences offer causes them to leave the STEM cluster. This seems plausible, as it is unlikely that receiving an offer from a STEM field reduces the probability of enrolling in any STEM field. The assumption also rules out a STEM offer inducing enrollment in a different STEM field from the one chosen following a non-STEM offer, such as a student who would enroll in Engineering following a Personal services offer but in Physical sciences following a Physical sciences offer. Second, Assumption 4 rules out students who enroll in different non-STEM fields depending on whether they receive a Physical sciences or Personal services offer. If receiving an offer from a STEM field does not make a student enroll into any STEM field, it is indeed unlikely that the offer induces enrollment into any non-STEM field instead.

Since the ISCED classification has more than two treatment clusters, identification requires Assumptions 3, 4, and 5. We discuss these assumptions in the context of the same example. Consider the next-best field of study Personal services in the cluster Services and the preferred field Physical sciences in the cluster Science. Similar to the two treatment cluster case, Assumption 3 ensures that receiving a Physical sciences offer does not make it less likely that a student enrolls into any Science field, and Assumption 4 prevents students who enroll in different non-Science fields depending on whether they receive a Physical sciences or Personal services offer. Assumption 5 additionally requires that a student enrolling into any Science field after receiving an offer from Physical sciences, does not enroll into any non-Services field when receiving an offer from Personal services. This is likely if the Services cluster represents a control group, as is the case for the sample of students with a next-best field in the Services cluster.

The validity of Assumptions 3 to 5 depends on whether clusters effectively group similar fields of study, such that students may update preferences and face low switching costs between fields within, but not across, treatment clusters. Wiswall and Zafar (2015) find evidence that student preferences are similar for majors within broad academic groups, suggesting that students initially enrolling in Physical sciences (Personal services) may later adjust their preferences towards related fields in Science (Services). Altonji et al. (2016) discuss that major-switching costs depend on a student’s education history. DGES (2015) describes that course changes in Portugal require an official request that includes potential accreditation of previous coursework. Since related fields share curricula, accreditation is often easier within clusters.

6.2 Results

6.2.1 Two treatment clusters: STEM and non-STEM

We find that STEM enrollment negatively impacts the number of achieved study credits in the second year. Table 5 shows that based on our estimates, STEM enrollment decreases ECTS on average by 3.15 credits for students preferring STEM over non-STEM in their course ranking. This decrease represents approximately 88 fewer hours of intended workload under STEM compared with non-STEM enrollment. The estimated effect is smaller for students preferring non-STEM over STEM: non-STEM enrollment increases ECTS on average by 1.33 credits for these students. The magnitude of this effect represents approximately 37 additional hours of intended workload. In case students are aware of the costs of STEM enrollment, their preference for and enrollment into STEM may be explained by other benefits, such as skill development or future monetary payoffs.

The estimates can be interpreted as weighted averages of LATEs between fields of study across the two treatment clusters. The STEM and non-STEM clusters include respectively 8 and 14 fields of study. The weighted averages include the LATEs corresponding to all possible pairs of fields across these two clusters, and for each of those field pairs all possible pairs of instruments between the two clusters. It follows that the treatment effect of STEM versus non-STEM (and vice versa) includes 8×14×8×14=12,5448\times 14\times 8\times 14=12,544 LATEs and corresponding weights.

The large and precisely estimated treatment take-up effects provide strong evidence that Assumption 2 holds for the STEM classification. Table 5 shows that, for students preferring a field in STEM over non-STEM, scoring above the cutoff and thereby receiving an offer from a STEM field increases the probability of enrollment in a STEM field by 88 percentage points. Conversely, for students preferring non-STEM over STEM, receiving a non-STEM offer increases the probability of non-STEM enrollment by 82 percentage points.

Since we have access to the data at the field of study level, we can also test the necessary conditions in Proposition 1 for a causal interpretation of the treatment cluster effects. We jointly test the (in)equalities in Proposition 1 within each sample defined by a preferred and next-best field using the clrtest package in Stata. Appendix C.4 provides further implementation details. Column (5) of Table 4 summarizes the testing results. After applying a Holm correction, we find no statistically significant violations of the necessary conditions for a causal interpretation of the estimated treatment cluster effects.

This result may be explained by most students having response types that can be described by (D⁡(j)=j,D⁡(k)=k)(D(j)=j,D(k)=k) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. Define πl​j​kh\pi_{ljk}^{h} as the coefficients πa​c​bh\pi_{acb}^{h} in (14) if each cluster contains only one treatment. The treatment take-up estimates for πl​j​kh\pi_{ljk}^{h} indeed suggest that most students enroll into their next-best or preferred field when they receive an offer from the next-best or preferred field, respectively. In particular, the average estimate of πj​j​kh\pi_{jjk}^{h} is 0.87, whereas the average absolute value of πl​j​kh\pi_{ljk}^{h} for l≠j,kl\neq j,k is 0.01. Together, these estimates leave little scope for response types that violate Assumptions 3 to 5 and reduce concerns about violations of the exclusion restriction. The full set of treatment take-up estimates at the field of study level is provided as supplementary data in the Supporting Information.

6.2.2 Multiple treatment clusters: Eight ISCED clusters

Table 6 shows the treatment cluster effect estimates across the eight ISCED clusters. After the Holm correction within each estimation sample, four estimates are statistically significant at the 5% level, compared with twelve before the correction. Their average absolute values are 4.13 and 3.44 ECTS, respectively. These effect sizes imply that some clustered fields can increase or decrease academic progress by the equivalent of approximately 100 hours of intended workload, or a medium-sized course.

For the ISCED classification, we also find strong evidence that Assumption 2 holds. Table 8 in Appendix C.5 reports the treatment take-up estimates for enrollment in the cluster containing the preferred field. Consistent with the evidence above that response types are predominantly characterized by (D⁡(j)=j,D⁡(k)=k)(D(j)=j,D(k)=k), these estimates are large and precise, generally ranging from 0.80 to 0.90.

We test the necessary conditions in Proposition 1 for the eight clusters and reject a causal interpretation of the treatment cluster effect estimates. Column (6) of Table 4 shows that we reject the necessary conditions for the fields Health and Personal services. These rejections do not affect the conditions for the STEM classification. For instance, the rejected conditions in the sample of next-best Personal services correspond to the preferred field Humanities, and both Personal services and Humanities belong to the non-STEM cluster. Appendix C.6 provides additional empirical results for both the STEM and ISCED classifications, also using the data at the field of study level.

7 Conclusion

Many modern policies involve multiple unordered treatments, for which many pairwise treatment comparisons are possible. A common approach is to aggregate these treatments into clusters and apply instrumental variable (IV) methods at the treatment cluster level.

This paper shows that IV methods with treatment clusters identify weighted averages of pairwise effects between treatments across clusters. The required assumptions are formulated at the unclustered treatment level and hence explicit about possible violations. We discuss how practitioners can justify these assumptions in the presence of treatment clusters and show that the assumptions are less strict compared to the assumptions required for identifying the pairwise effects between unclustered treatments. We also derive necessary conditions for these assumptions, and propose falsification tests for settings in which data at the unclustered treatment level is available.

We illustrate the empirical relevance of our methods by analyzing the causal effects of clusters of fields of study using a natural experiment in the Portuguese public higher education system. We consider the STEM versus non-STEM classification and eight clusters defined according to the International Standard Classification of Education. We find meaningful effects of enrollment in different clusters on study progress. Using data at the field of study level, we test the necessary conditions for causal interpretation of the treatment cluster effects.

=\displaystyle= ∑j∈Sa∑n∈Sc𝔼⁡[Dn|Z=j]​ℙ​[Z=j|Z∈Sa]−∑k∈Sb∑n∈Sc𝔼⁡[Dn|Z=k]​ℙ​[Z=k|Z∈Sb].\displaystyle\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{n\in S_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[D_{n}|Z=j\right]\mathbb{P}[Z=j|Z\in S_{a}]-\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{n\in S_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[D_{n}|Z=k\right]\mathbb{P}[Z=k|Z\in S_{b}].

Appendix B Additional theoretical results

Theorem 2 shows that the TSLS estimand identifies a weighted average of LATEs using only data at the clustered treatment level. When data at the unclustered treatment level is available, this Appendix provides three strategies for providing additional insights into the components of the weighted average. First, we show that the weights of the treatment effects are partially identified. Second, we consider two sets of additional assumptions which allow for the identification of both the weights and the LATEs in the weighted averages. We provide testable conditions for the additional assumptions.

B.1 Partial identification of the treatment effect weights

The contribution of each component λj​k​l​m​Δj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm}\Delta_{jklm} to βa​b\beta_{ab} is determined jointly by the LATE Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm} and its weight λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm}. These weights represent the normalized proportion of the response types corresponding to each LATE. From a policy perspective, these weights capture how policy-induced encouragement affects treatment take up. For instance, the weights illustrate how enrollment into specific non-STEM and STEM fields respond to a policy promoting female enrollment in STEM.

In the general case in which both SaS_{a} and SbS_{b} contain multiple treatments, these weights cannot be point identified. In this case, individuals observed to take a treatment from SaS_{a} if Z∈SaZ\in S_{a} could have taken any treatment in SbS_{b} if Z∈SbZ\in S_{b}, and the other way around.

Corollary 1 (Partial identification treatment effect weights).


Under Assumptions 1-5, it holds for λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm} in (5) with j,l∈Saj,l\in S_{a} and k,m∈Sbk,m\in S_{b} that

max⁡(0,−πm​j​k−∑n∈{Sa∖l}πn​j​k)​ωj​k∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sbωj​k​∑l∈Saπl​j​k≤λj​k​l​m≤min⁡(πl​j​k,−πm​j​k)​ωj​k∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sbωj​k​∑l∈Saπl​j​k,\displaystyle\frac{\max(0,-\pi_{mjk}-\sum_{n\in\{S_{a}\setminus l\}}\pi_{njk})\omega_{jk}}{\sum\limits_{j\in S_{a}}\sum\limits_{k\in S_{b}}\omega_{jk}\sum\limits_{l\in S_{a}}\pi_{ljk}}\leq\lambda_{jklm}\leq\frac{\min(\pi_{ljk},-\pi_{mjk})\omega_{jk}}{\sum\limits_{j\in S_{a}}\sum\limits_{k\in S_{b}}\omega_{jk}\sum\limits_{l\in S_{a}}\pi_{ljk}}, (44)

where πl​j​k=𝔼⁡[Dl|Z=j]−𝔼⁡[Dl|Z=k]=ℙ⁡[D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)≠l]−ℙ⁡[D⁡(j)≠l,D⁡(k)=l]\pi_{ljk}=\mathbb{E}[D_{l}|Z=j]-\mathbb{E}[D_{l}|Z=k]=\mathbb{P}[D(j)=l,D(k)\neq l]-\mathbb{P}[D(j)\neq l,D(k)=l], and ωj​k\omega_{jk} as defined in (6).

The proof is deferred to Appendix B.4. Corollary 1 provides individual bounds on each weight. These bounds do not jointly characterize the feasible weights, since extreme values for different weights may not be simultaneously attainable.

Corollary 1 shows that the proportion of types (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=l,D(k)=m) is upper bounded by both the total proportion of types (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)∈Sb)(D(j)=l,D(k)\in S_{b}) and the total proportion of types (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)=m). A lower bound is constructed by the difference between the total proportion of types (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)=m) and the total proportion of types (D⁡(j)∈{Sa∖l},D⁡(k)∈Sb)(D(j)\in\{S_{a}\setminus l\},D(k)\in S_{b}). Since πl​j​k\pi_{ljk} and ωj​k\omega_{jk} can be identified from unclustered treatment data, the bounds can be estimated when this data is observed.

When either SaS_{a} or SbS_{b} contains only one treatment, the bounds in Corollary 1 boil down to point identification. If Sa={j}S_{a}=\{j\}, the proportion of types with (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)=m) coincides with (D⁡(j)=j,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=j,D(k)=m), and if Sb={k}S_{b}=\{k\}, the proportion of types with (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)∈Sb)(D(j)=l,D(k)\in S_{b}) coincides with (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=k)(D(j)=l,D(k)=k). This yields the following expressions with Sa={j}S_{a}=\{j\} and Sb={k}S_{b}=\{k\}, respectively:

λj​k​j​m=−πm​j​k​ℙ​[Z=k|Z∈Sb]∑k∈Sbℙ⁡[Z=k|Z∈Sb]​πj​j​k​ and ​λj​k​l​k=πl​j​k​ℙ​[Z=j|Z∈Sa]∑j∈Saℙ⁡[Z=j|Z∈Sa]​∑l∈Saπl​j​k.\displaystyle\hskip-2.8903pt\lambda_{jkjm}=\frac{-\pi_{mjk}\mathbb{P}[Z=k|Z\in S_{b}]}{\sum\limits_{k\in S_{b}}\mathbb{P}[Z=k|Z\in S_{b}]\pi_{jjk}}\text{ and }\lambda_{jklk}=\frac{\pi_{ljk}\mathbb{P}[Z=j|Z\in S_{a}]}{\sum\limits_{j\in S_{a}}\mathbb{P}[Z=j|Z\in S_{a}]\sum\limits_{l\in S_{a}}\pi_{ljk}}. (45)

B.2 Full identification with heterogeneity restrictions

In addition to the treatment weights λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm}, we aim to identify the corresponding LATEs Δj​k​l​m\Delta_{jklm}. To achieve this, we specify the estimand that targets the LATEs Δj​k​j​k\Delta_{jkjk} for all jj comparing to treatment kk:

α𝐤=\displaystyle\mathbf{\alpha_{k}}= (α0​k,α1​k,…,αk−1,k,αk+1,k,…,αJ​k)′=𝔼​[𝐙𝐤​𝐃𝐤′]−1​𝔼​[𝐙𝐤​Y],\displaystyle(\alpha_{0k},\alpha_{1k},\dots,\alpha_{k-1,k},\alpha_{k+1,k},\dots,\alpha_{Jk})^{\prime}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{{Z_{k}}}\mathbf{{D_{k}}}^{\prime}]^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{{Z_{k}}}Y], (46)

which equals β𝐛\mathbf{\beta_{b}} if Sj={j}S_{j}=\{j\} for j=1,…,Jj=1,\dots,J with Sb={k}S_{b}=\{k\}. The corollary below shows that αj​k=Δj​k​j​k\alpha_{jk}=\Delta_{jkjk} when we impose restrictions on treatment effect heterogeneity.

Corollary 2 (Treatment effect heterogeneity restrictions).


Under Assumptions 1-5 and the following two conditions

  1. 1.

    If j∈Saj\in S_{a}, Δj​k​l​m=Δl​k​l​k−Δm​k​m​k\Delta_{jklm}=\Delta_{lklk}-\Delta_{mkmk} for l∈Sal\in S_{a} and k,m∈Sbk,m\in S_{b} for all a≠ba\neq b,

  2. 2.

    If j∈Sbj\in S_{b}, Δj​k​l​m=Δl​k​l​k−Δm​k​m​k\Delta_{jklm}=\Delta_{lklk}-\Delta_{mkmk} for k∈Sbk\in S_{b} and all l,m∈Sl,m\in S,

it holds that

βa​b=\displaystyle{\beta}_{ab}= ∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sb∑l∈SaΔl​k​l​k​πl​j​k​ωj​k∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sb∑l∈Saπl​j​k​ωj​k−∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sb∑m∈SbΔm​k​m​k​πm​j​k​ωj​k∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sb∑m∈Sbπm​j​k​ωj​k,\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{l\in S_{a}}\Delta_{lklk}\pi_{ljk}\omega_{jk}}{\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{l\in S_{a}}\pi_{ljk}\omega_{jk}}-\frac{\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{m\in S_{b}}\Delta_{mkmk}\pi_{mjk}\omega_{jk}}{\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\sum_{m\in S_{b}}\pi_{mjk}\omega_{jk}}, (47)
αj​k=\displaystyle\alpha_{jk}= Δj​k​j​k, with ​j∈Sa​ and ​k∈Sb.\displaystyle\Delta_{jkjk},\text{ with }j\in S_{a}\text{ and }k\in S_{b}. (48)

The proof is deferred to Appendix B.5. Assumptions 3 to 5 allow for response types (D⁡(j)∈Sa,D⁡(k)∈Sb)(D(j)\in S_{a},D(k)\in S_{b}) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. To identify αj​k\alpha_{jk}, we require restrictions on the effects between treatments across SaS_{a} and SbS_{b} for all a≠ba\neq b that correspond to these responses (condition 1). Since the responses to instrument values within SbS_{b} are not restricted, we additionally require restrictions on the treatment effects that correspond to these responses (condition 2). In case both conditions hold, the weighted average of αj​k\alpha_{jk} in (47) equals βa​b{\beta}_{ab}. Hence, the conditions are violated if the equality in (47) does not hold, and (47) thus serves as a necessary condition for the restrictions on treatment effect heterogeneity.

The restrictions in Corollary 2 are substantially stronger than those required for Theorem 1. Treatment effect heterogeneity is not allowed to be systematically related to individuals’ response types. A sufficient condition is mean independence of pairwise treatment effects from the potential treatment choices. This allows expected outcome levels to differ across response types, but requires the relative effects of fields of study not to depend on how students’ enrollment responds to field offers. Such restrictions may be more plausible when students have limited information about their field-specific gains, so that sorting on those gains is less likely and choices instead reflect access constraints or geographic considerations.

B.3 Full identification under response type restrictions

Alternatively, the LATEs can be identified by ruling out additional response types. Consider Assumptions 3 to 5, with each cluster only including one treatment, such that Sj={j}S_{j}=\{j\} for j=1,…,Jj=1,\dots,J. These assumptions only allow for response types with D⁡(j)≠D⁡(k)D(j)\neq D(k) that satisfy (D⁡(j)=j,D⁡(k)=k)(D(j)=j,D(k)=k) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. Thus, each instrument can only induce take up of its intended treatment.

Corollary 3 (Response type restrictions).


Under Assumption 1, and Assumption 2-5 at the unclustered treatment level, it holds that

βa​b=\displaystyle\beta_{ab}= ∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sbλj​k​j​k​Δj​k​j​k,λj​k​j​k=πj​j​k​ωj​k∑j∈Sa∑k∈Sbπj​j​k​ωj​k,\displaystyle\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\lambda_{jkjk}\Delta_{jkjk},\quad\lambda_{jkjk}=\frac{\pi_{jjk}\omega_{jk}}{\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\sum_{k\in S_{b}}\pi_{jjk}\omega_{jk}}, (49)
αj​k=\displaystyle\alpha_{jk}= Δj​k​j​k, with ​j∈Sa​ and ​k∈Sb.\displaystyle\Delta_{jkjk},\text{ with }j\in S_{a}\text{ and }k\in S_{b}. (50)

The proof is deferred to Section B.6. The assumptions in Corollary 3 imply that ϕj​j​kA≥0\phi_{jjk}^{A}\geq 0 and ϕl​j​kA=0\phi_{ljk}^{A}=0 for all l≠j,kl\neq j,k. Similar to Proposition 1 at the level of treatment clusters, these ϕl​j​kA\phi_{ljk}^{A} pose testable conditions for Assumptions 3 to 5 at the unclustered treatment level.

The conditions at the unclustered level are more demanding than their cluster-level counterparts: if they hold at the unclustered level, the corresponding cluster-level conditions also hold, but not vice versa. Similar conditions for identifying LATEs between unclustered treatments are discussed by Behaghel et al. (2013) and Bhuller and Sigstad (2024). In the context of fields of study, Kirkebøen et al. (2016) invoke Assumptions 2 to 5 at the unclustered level and subsequently aggregate fields into ten clusters in their empirical application. Corollary 3 shows that the resulting treatment cluster estimand identifies a weighted average of LATEs between individual fields.
