Appendix C Additional details empirical application

C.1 Deferred acceptance in Portugal

Each course has a quota (qq) of applicants that can be admitted, which are set in agreement between the institutions and the Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Ensino Superior (MCTES; Ministry of Science, Technology and Higher Education) and are relatively stable across years. Students submit their rankings to the Direção-Geral do Ensino Superior (DGES; Directorate General for Higher Education), which runs the centralized admission process. DGES ranks for each course the applicants by their application score. This score is a weighted average of an applicant’s high school and national exam grades. Since each course weighs the high school grades and the national exams differently, the application scores are applicant-course specific (Article 33 until 36 of DGES (2019)).

The applicants are matched to courses using an iterative process (Article 37 of DGES (2019)), similar to the college-proposing Gale-Shapley algorithm (Gale and Shapley, 1962):

  • •

    Step 1: Each course makes offers to the first qq applicants on its ranked list. Each applicant keeps the best offer according to her submitted ranking and rejects the rest.

  • •

    Step s≥2s\geq 2: Any course rejected in step s−1s-1 by n≥1n\geq 1 applicants proposes to the next nn applicants on its list. Each applicant keeps the best offer according to her submitted ranking among all the proposals received in step ss (including the one retained in step s−1s-1) and rejects the rest.

The algorithm terminates when the allocation is not updated, and matches each course to the set of qq most preferred applicants who did not reject it.

One to two weeks before the start of the academic year, each applicant receives the offer from her matched course. Within that week, applicants have to accept the offer, participate in a second cycle, or withdraw from the application process. The slots that have remained or were not accepted after the first cycle are then allocated to the applicants who participate in the second cycle according to the same algorithm. The process concludes with an identical third cycle.

C.2 Data

We use data from two different sources. First, the higher education application data from DGES contains for each applicant the submitted course ranking, their application scores, the matched course, and the course cutoffs, from 2008-09 to 2019-20. We consider for each student the first cycle from the earliest observed application in which the student also enrolls in the first year. We refer to students who applied in that cycle within the same year as a cohort.

The second data set has the student outcome data from the Direção-Geral de Estatísticas da Educação e Ciência (DGEEC; Directorate for Education Statistics). For each enrolled student, this data set contains the enrolled course, whether the student is active in the first, second, or third year of that course, and the achieved number of ECTS study credits in that course in the previous year, from 2013-14 to 2019-20. Our main treatment and outcome variable are enrollment and ECTS credits in the second year of a course. In case a student is active in the second year of a course across multiple years, these variables will refer to the first observed enrollment in the second year of a course.

The student outcome data can be merged to the application data if we observe a student’s enrollment in the first year. Hence, the first cohort for which we can combine the data sets is 2013-14. We take 2016-17 as the final cohort, so that we can use course enrollment in the second year up to 2018-19, allowing for a one-year delay. This results in the final data set with four cohorts from 2013-14 unto 2016-17.

To arrive at the final estimation sample, we implement the procedure described in Section 6.1.1 to select applicants with a (locally) preferred and next-best field of study, and exclude a small subset of 751 applicants (representing 1.50% of the remaining applicants). The excluded applicants are characterized by a combination of preferred and next-best unclustered fields of study with (1) fewer than 10 observations, (2) perfect compliance, where all applicants above (below) the cutoff are enrolled in the preferred (next-best) field in second year, or (3) exact multicollinearity, where all applicants score either above or below the cutoff. The preferred and next-best field combinations with perfect compliance and exact multicollinearity make the estimation of the IV model in (13)-(14) impossible.

Panel A of Table 7 shows descriptive statistics of the final estimation sample. This sample includes 27.24 percent of the total number of applicants in the four cohorts. The mean of the running variable is positive, and 68% of the students are assigned to their preferred field. The applicants have on average 5.46 courses on their course ranking. In 88% of these rankings, the top two fields equal our measure for the preferred and next-best field. The enrolled field in year two is different from the initially matched field for 8% of the students. The mean of second-year ECTS across all enrolled students is equal to 54.19. However, there is substantial variation in the number of ECTS between fields. For instance, students enrolled in Physical sciences and Architecture and building have a mean second-year ECTS of less than 50, those in Law and Social and behavioural science have a mean of around 53, and students in Health and Journalism and information have a mean of almost 60.

Panel B of Table 7 provides an overview of the most common preferred fields for each next-best. All 22 next-best fields have a skewed distribution of students across preferred fields. For instance, 77.83% (16.64%) of the students with Computing as next-best prefer Engineering (Business and administration). The remaining 5.53% prefer any of the other 19 fields. Panel B also shows that the number of observations differs across next-best fields. For example, there are 7,432 students with Business and administration as next-best versus 363 students with Agriculture, forestry and fishery.

C.3 Robustness checks and validity of the continuity assumption

We assess the robustness of our results against more flexible specifications. In our baseline specification, we use a polynomial of degree one, so that fh​(S)=γ​Sf_{h}(S)=\gamma S, and do not apply a bandwidth. First, we include an additional interaction term between SS and an indicator for scoring above the cutoff across all preferred fields (∑c≠bZ~c\sum_{c\neq b}\tilde{Z}_{c}) in (14). Second, we include S2S^{2} as an additional control variable in both (13) and (14). Third, we assess the robustness of our results via the use of symmetric bandwidths equal to 40, 30, and 20. These bandwidths include 94.59%, 87.02%, and 70.94% of the total sample respectively.

Panel A of Figure 1 presents the results of these robustness checks using the unclustered fields of study. Specifically, the left plot compares the treatment take-up estimates from (14) of our baseline specification with those from each robustness check. The estimates lie close to the 45-degree line, indicating virtually identical results across all specifications. Similarly, the right plot illustrates that the treatment effect estimates from (13) are similar across the robustness checks. The largest deviation occurs with a bandwidth of 20, which also substantially reduces statistical power and weakens the significance. Panels B and C of Figure 1 confirm that these conclusions continue to hold when using the STEM and the ISCED classification.

Next, we assess the validity of the local continuity assumption (Assumption 6). First, we examine whether the application score to the next-best field is continuous at the cutoff. Figure 2 plots the maximum score across all courses in the preference block of the next-best field against the running variable. Consistent with continuous potential outcomes, this score does not show a discontinuity around the cutoff. This result is confirmed with a pooled regression on the students from all next-best fields: We regress the application score to the next-best field on the running variable and a single treatment dummy indicating whether students scored above the cutoff, and the estimate on this treatment dummy is equal to -0.31 and has a pp-value of 0.17. The application score is the only background characteristic we observe for all students.

Second, we examine the density of the students across all next-best fields near the course cutoffs (McCrary, 2008). If applicants have precise control over their application score, we might observe bunching just above the cutoffs and the local continuity assumption may not be valid (Lee and Lemieux, 2010). However, Figure 3 shows no sign of excess mass just above the cutoffs. The bias corrected discontinuity test introduced in Cattaneo, Jansson, and Ma (2018) has a test statistic equal to 0.13 with a pp-value of 0.90, implying that we cannot reject the null hypothesis of no discontinuity.

The continuity assumption is also consistent with the setting at hand. The number of applications is different each year, and hence the cutoffs change from year to year and are unknown at the time of application. The cutoffs only become publicly available when the applicants receive their offer. A regression of the cutoffs across years on course dummies has an R-squared of 0.82, which confirms the movement in the cutoffs across years.

C.4 Testing the necessary conditions

The (in)equalities ϕl​j​kA⋚0\phi^{A}_{ljk}\lesseqgtr 0 in Proposition 1 can be written as conditional moment inequalities with YY as the conditioning variable instead of ZZ. In particular, the inequality ϕl​j​kA≥0\phi^{A}_{ljk}\geq 0 with l,j∈Sal,j\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b} can be written as

𝔼⁡[𝕀Y∈A​Dl|Z=k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}|Z=k] ≤𝔼⁡[𝕀Y∈A​Dl|Z=j]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}|Z=j] (69)
𝔼[𝕀Y∈ADlZk]ℙ[Z=j]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}Z_{k}]\mathbb{P}[Z=j] ≤𝔼[𝕀Y∈ADlZj]ℙ[Z=k]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}Z_{j}]\mathbb{P}[Z=k]
𝔼[cjDlZk−\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c_{j}D_{l}Z_{k}- ckDlZj|Y=y]≤0,\displaystyle c_{k}D_{l}Z_{j}|Y=y]\leq 0,

where cj=ℙ[Z=j]c_{j}=\mathbb{P}[Z=j], and the last line follows from Mourifié and Wan (2017). Similarly, the inequality ϕl​j​kA≤0\phi^{A}_{ljk}\leq 0 with l,k∈Sbl,k\in S_{b} and j∈Saj\in S_{a} can be written as

𝔼⁡[𝕀Y∈A​Dl|Z=j]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}|Z=j] ≤𝔼⁡[𝕀Y∈A​Dl|Z=k]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{I}_{Y\in A}D_{l}|Z=k] (70)
𝔼[ckDlZj−\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[c_{k}D_{l}Z_{j}- cjDlZk|Y=y]≤0.\displaystyle c_{j}D_{l}Z_{k}|Y=y]\leq 0.

For the equality ϕl​j​kA=0\phi^{A}_{ljk}=0 with l∉{Sa,Sb}l\notin\{S_{a},S_{b}\}, j∈Saj\in S_{a}, and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}, both (69) and (70) must hold.

These conditional moment inequalities can be tested using the intersection bounds framework of Chernozhukov et al. (2013), implemented in the Stata package clrtest by Chernozhukov et al. (2015). The clrtest allows for the joint testing of inequalities within an estimation sample. Hence, within each sample defined by a preferred and next-best field (j,k)(j,k) at the unclustered fields of study level, we jointly test the restrictions on ϕl​j​kA\phi^{A}_{ljk} for all treatments ll.

For example, similar to the discussion of the identifying assumptions in Section 6.1.4, consider testing the STEM classification with Personal services as the next-best field (kk) in the non-STEM cluster. In this case there are 8 preferred STEM fields (jj), such as Physical sciences. An offer from jj instead of kk can weakly increase enrollment in the 8 STEM fields according to (69), and weakly decrease it in the 14 non-STEM fields according to (70).

Now consider testing the ISCED classification. Again take the next-best field Personal services (kk), which now belongs to the Services cluster, and the preferred field Physical sciences (jj), which belongs to the Science cluster. In this case an offer from jj instead of kk can weakly increase enrollment in the 4 fields belonging to the Science cluster according to (69), weakly decrease it in the 4 fields in the Services cluster according to (70), and should have no effect on the 14 fields in the other clusters according to (69) and (70).

To account for multiple testing within each next-best field kk, we follow Mourifié and Wan (2017) and apply the Holm (1979) correction to multiple applications of clrtest across different samples. The Holm procedure orders the pp-values within each next-best field and compares them to adjusted significance levels α\alpha divided by their rank. Rejections stop once a pp-value exceeds its threshold. Because clrtest does not report pp-values directly, we retrieve them by evaluating the test over a fine grid of confidence intervals in [0.90,1)[0.90,1), constructed with step sizes that decrease from 10−310^{-3} to 10−1210^{-12} as the grid approaches 1.

The clrtest package allows both nonparametric and parametric estimation of the conditional moment inequalities. We use the parametric option, which approximates the conditional expectations using a linear regression in YY. This is preferable in our setting because the estimation samples (j,k)(j,k) can be small, making nonparametric estimation less reliable.

The inequalities are evaluated over values of the conditioning variable YY. In our application YY corresponds to the number of ECTS credits. We evaluate the inequalities for values of YY between the 20th percentile (48 ECTS) and the 80th percentile (60 ECTS), in increments of 1 ECTS, avoiding extreme outcome values.

We implement the tests without including the running variable. Since the inequalities are intended to hold locally at the application score cutoff, this corresponds to the local randomization approach to RDDs (Cattaneo et al., 2024). In the baseline test we use the full sample, as in the main RDD analysis. As a robustness check we also repeat the tests using symmetric bandwidths of 40, 30, and 20. The results are similar.

C.5 Treatment take-up estimates with ISCED classification

We analyze the treatment take-up estimates for the ISCED classification. Estimating (14) yields a matrix of treatment take-up effects for each treatment cluster SbS_{b}. For each combination of clusters SaS_{a} and SbS_{b} containing the preferred and next-best fields, respectively, Table 8 reports only the effect of receiving an offer from the preferred field on enrollment in a field from cluster SaS_{a}. Most estimates are large and precise, ranging from 0.80 to 0.90. Thus, scoring above the cutoff and receiving an offer from the preferred field raises the probability of enrollment in the cluster containing that field by 80 to 90 percentage points. The smallest estimate is 0.59 for students preferring a field in Health and welfare over one in Agriculture. Overall, these results provide strong evidence that Assumption 2 holds for the ISCED classification.

C.6 Additional empirical results

This section applies the results derived in Appendix B to the field of study level data to provide additional information about the weights and LATEs underlying the estimated treatment cluster effects. The required treatment take-up estimates πl​j​kh\pi_{ljk}^{h} from (14) and treatment effect estimates βj​kh\beta_{jk}^{h} from (13) at the unclustered field of study level are provided as supplementary data in the Supporting Information. Because we do not conduct statistical inference on the estimated bounds or weighted averages, we use them only to describe patterns in our sample and draw no conclusions about their population-level counterparts.

C.6.1 Two treatment clusters: STEM and non-STEM

We estimate the bounds on the weights in Corollary 1 by replacing the treatment take-up estimands πl​j​k\pi_{ljk} and the relevant probabilities with their sample analogues. This yields estimated bounds for the 12,544 treatment effect weights between the STEM and non-STEM clusters. The left plot in Figure 4 shows a scatterplot of the estimated upper bounds against the estimated lower bounds for the weights λj​k​l​m\lambda_{jklm}. The black (gray) markers correspond to the weights with j=lj=l and k=mk=m (j≠lj\neq l and/or k≠mk\neq m). The estimated bounds are tight and suggest that most weight is assigned to response types (D⁡(j)=j,D⁡(k)=k)(D(j)=j,D(k)=k) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. For instance, the treatment cluster effect estimate of non-STEM versus STEM consists for 30% of the LATE of Health versus Life sciences with offers from respectively Health and Life sciences, another 22% is attributed to Health versus Engineering and engineering trades with offers from respectively Health and Engineering and engineering trades, and 10% to Arts versus Architecture and building with offers from respectively Arts and Architecture and building.

We next examine the assumptions that allow for the identification of the LATEs within the weighted averages. Corollaries 2 and 3 show that the LATEs are identified by αj​k\alpha_{jk} in (46) under treatment effect heterogeneity restrictions or additional response type restrictions, respectively. Under either set of restrictions, the treatment cluster effects between STEM and non-STEM equal a weighted average of identifiable LATEs. We estimate these weighted averages by replacing the treatment take-up and LATE estimands, πl​j​k\pi_{ljk} and αj​k\alpha_{jk}, and the relevant probabilities with their sample analogues. The right plot in Figure 4 plots the estimated weighted average under treatment effect heterogeneity restrictions from Corollary 2 against the estimated treatment cluster effects with 95% confidence intervals. The left plot of Figure 5 shows these estimates under response type restrictions from Corollary 3. In both figures, the confidence intervals overlap with the 45-degree line. One explanation for this result may be that treatment effect heterogeneity is restricted. However, it may be more likely that the weighted averages of LATEs assign little weight to the response types (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=l,D(k)=m) with j≠lj\neq l and/or k≠mk\neq m.

The necessary conditions and the weighted average of LATEs suggest that the estimates according to (46) provide a reasonable approximation to the LATEs in the treatment cluster effects. Hence, we can further unpack the treatment cluster effects. For instance, the non-STEM versus STEM treatment cluster effect (1.33 credits) comprises 30% from Health versus Life sciences (-0.03 credits), 22% from Health versus Engineering and engineering trades (1.08 credits), and 10% from Arts versus Architecture and building (5.02 credits). With an average absolute value of the estimated LATEs of 4,6284,628 ECTS credits, all ten estimates with Environmental protection as next-best field are considered unreliable and set to zero when constructing the weighted average of LATEs in Corollaries 2 and 3.

C.6.2 Multiple treatment clusters: Eight ISCED clusters

We bound the weights for the treatment effects between the eight clusters. The left plot in Figure 6 shows the estimated weights when the next-best field belongs to the Science cluster, allowing us to distinguish between the seven clusters containing the preferred fields. As with the STEM clusters, the estimated bounds are tight and suggest that most weight is assigned to response types (D⁡(j)=j,D⁡(k)=k)(D(j)=j,D(k)=k) with j∈Saj\in S_{a} and k∈Sbk\in S_{b}. For instance, the treatment cluster effect for Social sciences, business and law versus Science consists for 22% of the LATE of Business and administration versus Computing with offers from respectively Business and administration and Computing. Another 17% is attributed to Business and administration versus Mathematics and statistics with offers from Business and administration and Mathematics and statistics, and 16% to Social and behavioural science versus Life sciences with offers from Social and behavioural science and Life sciences.

We examine the additional assumptions to identify the LATEs within the treatment cluster effects. The right plot in Figure 6 plots the estimated weighted average of LATEs against the treatment effects between the ISCED clusters using treatment effect heterogeneity restrictions. The right plot of Figure 5 shows these estimates under the response type restrictions. Similar to the results with the STEM clusters, the 95% confidence intervals of the treatment cluster effects overlap with the 45-degree line. This may indicate negligible bias in the identification of the LATEs due to little treatment effect heterogeneity or little weight to the response types (D⁡(j)=l,D⁡(k)=m)(D(j)=l,D(k)=m) with j≠lj\neq l and/or k≠mk\neq m.

In this case, the estimated LATEs corresponding to the 22 fields of study can be used to provide further insights into the treatment cluster effects. For instance, the estimated treatment cluster effect of Social sciences, business and law versus Science (3.49 credits) comprises 22% from Business and administration versus Computing (2.60 credits), 17% from Business and administration versus Mathematics and statistics (6.69 credits), and 16% from Social and behavioural science versus Life sciences (4.87 credits).
